summary:
Private, non-commercial sexual relations between consenting same-sex adults aged 16 and over have been lawful in Cuba since 1979, when the Social Defence Code that treated homosexual practices as a social threat was repealed. The offence of public display of homosexual condition was repealed in 1987. The offence of bothering or soliciting with homosexual requests was amended in 1997 to refer only to sexual requests.

Article 42 of the 2019 Constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. It was the first constitutional text to name both grounds expressly. The definition of marriage as between a man and a woman in Article 36 was removed in the February 2019 referendum, with marriage defined on the basis of free will and equality of rights.

Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation is unlawful in Cuba. Discrimination on the basis of gender identity is also unlawful. In employment, Law 116 and the labour amendment approved in December 2013 bar discrimination on sexual orientation. Article 2(b) of the Labour Code covers orientation and does not list gender identity as a separate protected ground.

Following the Family Code referendum on 25 September 2022, Cuba recognises same-sex marriage and unions, same-sex adoption and non-commercial surrogacy. The referendum proposal also included codified domestic-violence penalties and shared parental rights. The Code confirms that legal gender change does not require surgery.

Transgender health care is provided within the public health system under Resolution 126 of 2008.

Police received orders in 1988 not to harass lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons after repeal of the 1938 Public Ostentation Law. In 2001 police prevented gay and trans persons from meeting in the street, fined them and closed meeting places. In 2004 police conducted a campaign directed at travestis and arrested persons dressed in women's clothing.

Since 1993 lesbian, gay and bisexual persons and transgender persons may serve openly in the Cuban Revolutionary Armed Forces.

Pride parades are held in Havana every May to coincide with the International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia, with attendance growing each year. Cuba voted in 2016, 2019, 2022 and 2025 in favour of renewing the mandate of the United Nations independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
Between 1965 and 1968 gay men were sent to UMAP forced-labour camps, where conscripts cut cane in Camagüey for about 60 hours per week for seven pesos a day and were subjected to electric-shock and injection experiments presented as cures. A political turning point was declared in 1975. In a 2010 interview with La Jornada, Fidel Castro accepted personal blame for that persecution.

The state-backed sexual-education programme led by CENESEX has campaigned for lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender acceptance since the late 2000s, including a trans-rights campaign, sexual-diversity education and work with the police and the Supreme Court.

The 25 September 2022 Family Code referendum was only the fourth national vote since 1959. Religious opponents objected on doctrinal grounds. Others feared child-welfare provisions could be used against dissidents. Some opponents of the government planned to vote No to deny the Díaz-Canel administration a victory amid the crackdown following the July 2021 protests, in which more than 1,400 people were arrested, and record emigration. The equality settlement remains contested.
localsOnly:
The December 2013 employment protection followed intense parliamentary debate. Mariela Castro of CENESEX proposed extending the ban to cover gender identity, disability and HIV status. That trans-inclusive proposal drew support from some Christian and intellectual legislators, but the confirmed outcome was a ban on sexual-orientation discrimination.

In 2012 Adela Hernández won election as delegate to the City Council of Caibarién in Villa Clara province, the first known transgender person to hold public office in Cuba.

Cuban authorities have charged lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex citizens who flee to seek asylum with treason and treason against the homeland. Víctor Manuel Dueñas and Onasis Torres faced up to eight years in prison if returned after filing asylum claims in the Netherlands in January 2018. A woman deported from the Netherlands was detained on 19 May 2018. Activists including Nelson Gandulla of the Cuban LGBTI Equality Foundation remained under monitoring.
outOfScopeNotes:
Not sourced in the inventory are the administrative steps a visitor would follow to change a name or gender marker, and whether short-term visitors can access trans-related care in the public system.

Unresolved is whether any statute regulates access to toilets or other sex-segregated facilities for transgender persons, and whether hate-crime provisions add penalties for bias based on sexual orientation or gender identity.

Unresolved is current street-level police practice toward transgender visitors beyond the 1988 non-harassment orders and the 2001 and 2004 campaigns, and whether entry, visa or border-screening rules create a distinct risk of outing.
